verses.translation_literal: A song of the ascents. How blessed [is] every fearer of YHWH, the one walking in his ways.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song for the climbing road. Happy, happy the one who stands in awe of the LORD, whose feet keep to the paths he has laid down.
verses.directors_commentary:
The opening word, 'ashrei, is not a polite 'blessed is' but an exclamation: how happy, how fortunate! It is the same cry that opens Psalm 1 and is the voice of a crowd greeting a neighbour who is doing well. The KJV's 'Blessed' flattens it into a pious statement; the pilgrims singing it on the road to Jerusalem are congratulating someone. Note the sweep of 'every' (kol): the promise is open to any person who fears YHWH, and Rashi on Psalms 128:1 observes that 'every' is deliberately wider than 'the man' of Psalms 1:1 and 112:1, to include the woman.

See also the KJV's 'Song of degrees': 'degrees' is the old word for steps. The Hebrew ma'alot is 'ascents', the stairs, the road up to Jerusalem, or the pilgrim journey itself. 'Fear' here is awe and obedience, not terror. Ibn Ezra and Radak read 'fears' as avoiding what is forbidden and 'walks' as doing what is commanded, a pair that the verse's two participles invite.

philological_notes.note: A plural construct, an exclamation of congratulation ('oh the happiness of...'), not a blessing formula. It describes someone's good state, where barukh would call down God's favour.

'The ascents': the climbs or steps. The fifteen psalms (120-134) that carry this heading were sung on pilgrimage up to Jerusalem; the Targum renders it 'a song said over the steps of the abyss', a different tradition.
'Fearer of YHWH': awe, reverence and obedience. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David take the fear as avoiding the prohibitions and the walking as doing the commands.

verses.translation_literal: The toil of your palms, for you will eat [it]: how blessed are you, and it will be good to you.
verses.translation_dramatic: The labour of your own hands, you will eat it. Happy are you, and all will go well with you.
verses.directors_commentary:
In a subsistence economy of barley fields, vineyards and flocks, the great fear was that someone else would eat what you had grown: a raiding army, a tax collector, a creditor, a landlord. Deuteronomy 28:33 curses a people whose fruit 'a nation you do not know shall eat'. Against that fear, to eat the yield of your own work is the whole blessing.

The Hebrew is blunt: yegia' kappeikha, the 'toil' of 'your palms'. The KJV's 'labour of thine hands' is fair, but 'hands' is kappayim, the cupped palms, the working surface of the hand, and yegia' is the weariness the work leaves behind. The 'for' (ki) is also weaker than in English: it can mean 'when' or 'surely'. Rashi on Psalms 128:2 cites the Talmud (Berakhot 8a): whoever lives from his own labour inherits both worlds. Note the shift to the singular 'you': the psalm turns from a general 'every one' to one man at his table.

philological_notes.note: Toil, and the product of toil: what is won by effort that leaves one tired. Malbim reads the verse as limiting the work to what is needed to eat, not to grow rich.
Two clauses: the congratulation, then 'it will be good for you'. Radak, from the rabbis, assigns the first to this world and the second to the world to come.

verses.translation_literal: Your wife [will be] like a fruitful vine in the innermost parts of your house; your sons like shoots of olive trees around your table.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your wife, a vine heavy with fruit, deep in the heart of your house. Your sons, young olive shoots, crowded all around your table.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a picture of a house at mealtime, and every element is concrete. The vine is the Israelite's emblem of abundance and joy; a fruitful vine means children. yarkete bayit, 'the innermost parts', uses the word for 'flank' or 'thigh' (Metzudat Zion compares 'the thigh of the altar', Leviticus 4): it is the back or the side of the house, the sheltered interior. The KJV's 'by the sides of thine house' turns an interior into the outside wall and loses the point: she is within, safe, at the heart of things. Radak and Meiri tell of a vine planted inside the house with its branches trained out to the sun, so that the root is indoors and the fruit visible outside. That is a rabbinic reading of her modesty and public renown, not something the verse states.

The olive is the other staple tree. A young olive shoot (shetil) is a sucker planted at the base of the parent tree, and the sons grow in a ring about it. The Hebrew says 'sons', banekha; the KJV's 'children' softens it, and the ASV and BBE do the same. A table (shulchan) in the ancient house was a low mat or tray, so 'around' is literal: they sit pressed in around the father. The wife is addressed as 'your wife', in a psalm written for a male head of household, and the picture is of his world as he would have seen it.

philological_notes.note: The dual construct of yarkah, 'flank, far side, recess', related to yarekh 'thigh'. It means the rear or inner part of the house, not its outer side. Metzudat Zion compares 'on the thigh of the altar' (Leviticus 4).
'Like shoots of olives', the young plants set out around the parent. Rashi and Radak add that the olive does not take a graft, as a figure of children without taint; this is a traditional extension.

verses.translation_literal: Behold, for thus will a man be blessed, a fearer of YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look. This is how it is with the man who stands in awe of the LORD: this is how he is blessed.
verses.directors_commentary:
A pause for emphasis after the family picture. Hinneh, 'behold', points the audience back to the table just described: this, and nothing less, is what blessing looks like. The psalm shifts from 'every fearer' (v. 1) to gaver, 'a man' or 'strong man', the word for a man in his full strength and standing, and closes the ring by repeating 'fearer of YHWH' from verse 1.

The KJV's 'that thus shall the man be blessed' is stiff, and its clumsy 'that' is its attempt at the doubled particle ki-khen, 'for thus'. Note also the passive: the one who blesses is not named here. Meiri and Malbim take this verse as the end of the first half of the psalm, the blessing of the man himself and his household, before the focus widens to Zion and Israel.

philological_notes.note: A Pual imperfect, 'he will be blessed' (passive), against the active Piel 'may he bless' (yevarekh) of verse 5. The two verbs are one root and the shift from passive to active is deliberate.
A man in his strength, as against 'adam or 'ish. Used here for the head of the household.

verses.translation_literal: May YHWH bless you from Zion, and see the good of Jerusalem all the days of your life.
verses.translation_dramatic: May the LORD bless you out of Zion. And may your eyes rest on the good of Jerusalem, all the days of your life.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice changes. Up to now the psalm has described; now a priest or the assembled pilgrims speak a blessing over the man, as in the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24: yevarekhkha YHWH, 'may YHWH bless you'. The blessing comes 'from Zion', the mountain where the LORD's house stood and the sanctuary the pilgrims are approaching, as Psalm 134:3 also says. Rashi on Psalms 128:5 links Zion with Jacob's 'gate of heaven' (Genesis 28:17).

The KJV makes both halves a prediction ('shall bless', 'shalt see'). The Hebrew form is a wish, and the second verb is an imperative, 'see!', a command that works as a blessing: let this be your portion. For an exile or a farmer far away, 'see the good of Jerusalem' means to make the pilgrimage and share its festival joy; Ibn Ezra reads it as going up three times a year, Rashi cites Deuteronomy 26:11, 'you shall rejoice in all the good'. Radak reads it as the return from exile.

philological_notes.note: 'From Zion': the source of blessing is the sanctuary hill. The pilgrim is the one receiving it at the end of his climb.
'See in the good of': ra'ah with the preposition be- means to look upon with enjoyment and take part in, not merely to glimpse. The same phrase is in Psalm 27:13.

verses.translation_literal: And see sons of your sons: peace upon Israel.
verses.translation_dramatic: And may you live to see your children's children. Peace upon Israel.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends on two short blessings, the second only two words long in the Hebrew: shalom 'al Yisra'el, 'peace upon Israel'. The same cry closes Psalm 125. In a world where a plague, a famine or a raid could cut a family off, to see grandchildren was proof that the line had survived and the land could bear it. 'Sons of your sons' (banim levanekha) repeats 'sons' within one phrase: the household has grown by one generation.

The KJV's 'Yea, thou shalt see' adds a promise and a 'yea' the Hebrew does not have; the ASV and BBE are closer, setting the last phrase apart as its own wish. The jump from the old man's grandchildren to the nation is the point: the family's peace is the peace of Israel. Rashi's remark (on Psalms 128:6) ties this to inheritance and levirate marriage, a tradition about family quarrels. Malbim reads it as the grandchildren working for the whole people.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'sons to your sons', an idiom for grandchildren. The lamed marks the sons as belonging to your sons.
A verbless clause, either a wish ('peace be upon') or the thing seen. Metzudat David reads it as the imperative's second object: see Israel at peace on their own land.
